texto_fonte:
Common nutritional supplement may boost psoriasis treatment, small patient trial suggests
Researchers in China have discovered that the vitamin B5 derivative pantethine limits the activity of immune cells that are key contributors to autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis. The study, published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine, shows that pantethine prevents the development of psoriasis in mice and also helps alleviate the symptoms of psoriasis patients in a small-scale human trial.
Dendritic cells are specialized immune cells that help to coordinate the different parts of the immune system. They can engulf and present foreign antigens to activate highly specific T cells, as well as secrete a variety of immune signaling molecules to recruit other types of immune cells and promote inflammation. Because of this central role in directing immune responses, aberrant activation of dendritic cells is thought to underlie a variety of autoimmune diseases, including psoriasis.
"Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored."
Zhang co-led the new study with Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.
A metabolic link to immune overactivation
Zhang and colleagues found that the levels of metabolic enzymes known as Vanins are elevated in the dendritic cells of patients with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. Depleting these enzymes inhibited dendritic cell activation and limited their ability to activate T cells. Moreover, treating mice with a drug that inhibits Vanins prevented the animals from developing psoriasis.
Vanin enzymes convert the metabolite pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient required for cellular energy production. Pantethine itself is a widely available nutritional supplement often used to lower blood cholesterol levels due to its ability to inhibit cholesterol synthesis. Cholesterol can promote the activation of dendritic cells, and high blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for the development of psoriasis.
Zhang and colleagues determined that increased Vanin activity in dendritic cells reduces pantethine levels, leading to increased cholesterol synthesis and dendritic cell hyperactivation. Replenishing pantethine levels reversed this process, lowering the accumulation of cholesterol and suppressing dendritic cell activation.
"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang says.
Small trial suggests an added benefit
The researchers therefore initiated a small-scale trial of pantethine supplementation in 24 human psoriasis patients. Every patient was treated with topical calcipotriene/betamethasone ointment, but half of the patients also received pantethine tablets. Over the course of 12 weeks, patients given the additional pantethine treatment showed improved symptoms, particularly if they had elevated blood cholesterol levels to begin with.
"Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof of concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang says.
"Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholesterol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell–mediated autoimmune diseases."
Publication details
Cao et al. Vanin-pantethine metabolic axis shapes dendritic cell function and affects inflammatory disorder progression, Journal of Experimental Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1084/jem.20252558
Journal information: Journal of Experimental Medicine

candidato.titulo: How vaccines could be about to revolutionise acne treatments
candidato.resumo: Acne could be caused by our immune systems overreacting to proteins released by skin bacteria. Columnist Michael Le Page looks into the experimental treatments aiming to block this process and prevent or reduce acne

texto_fonte:
It’s a cruel twist. Just as we become more concerned about our appearance, our faces start to erupt in great red spots. Pimples cause anguish for many teenagers and can persist into adulthood too. But now two companies are developing vaccines that they hope will revolutionise the treatment of acne. Is an end to the misery at hand?
The main idea behind this new approach is that acne is caused by the immune system overreacting to proteins released by skin bacteria. Triggering the body to produce antibodies against these proteins should block this process and prevent – or at least reduce – acne. Pharma giant Sanofi is preparing for trials in the US and Canada of an mRNA vaccine targeting at least one bacterial protein, while US start-up Armora Biosciences is focusing on a different protein.
Better treatments for acne are certainly needed. “Acne causes a significant emotional burden,” says Tomasz Zastawny at Armora. “It can lead to the development of depression, social isolation and other psychological outcomes as well.”
Advertisement
It has been known for decades that acne is linked to the presence of a bacterium called Cutibacterium acnes, which thrives deep in hair follicles where there is little oxygen. But C. acnes is the most common skin bacterium, present on just about everybody – including those that don’t have acne – so there’s a lot more to it.
One factor is the surge in hormones during puberty, which increases the production of fatty substances in the skin, affecting bacterial growth. But not everyone gets pimply during adolescence, so there seem to be genetic factors involved as well.
“Acne is very complicated. It’s not an infection,” says Richard Gallo at the University of California, San Diego. “It’s an immune problem.”
In other words, while the presence of C. acne doesn’t usually cause problems, sometimes it may trigger a strong immune response inside a follicle. During this response, some cells in the skin actually turn into fat cells and start releasing alarm signals and antimicrobial substances – a process known as reactive adipogenesis. “This is a normal way to fight an infection, but in this case, it’s an inappropriate response,” says Gallo.
What triggers that response? C. acnes can secrete a toxin known as Christie-Atkins-Munch-Petersen factor, or CAMP. The bacteria may ramp up production of CAMP in certain circumstances.
So, Gallo’s team tried vaccinating mice against CAMP, to make the animals produce antibodies that neutralise the toxin. A number of studies by his team suggest this could help prevent or treat acne.
Sanofi has now developed an mRNA vaccine that targets CAMP, possibly along with some other C. acnes proteins – the company hasn’t revealed exactly what’s in the vaccine and, after much back and forth, declined to talk to me about it.
While there have been reports that the Sanofi trial is already underway, it is labelled as “not yet recruiting” as per the latest update on 18 September. This means it may be some time before we know if it works. That said, while these initial trials are primarily intended to establish safety, it should be clear to volunteers within weeks if it is making a difference to their acne – this isn’t like a normal vaccine trial where researchers have to wait months or years for people to be exposed to pathogens.
“We were very, very optimistic that this could be revolutionary for acne therapy,” says Gallo. “We’ll just have to see if it pans out in the human population.”
Meanwhile, Armora is targeting a different protein, called hyaluronidase, based on work by George Liu at the University of California, San Diego. Hyaluronidase is an enzyme that breaks down hyaluronic acid, a large sugar secreted into the spaces between cells. These terms might be familiar because hyaluronic acid is often used as a filler for cosmetic purposes, while hyaluronidase is injected to break down filler that is no longer wanted or if things go wrong.
Some bacteria such as strep B (Streptococcus agalactiae) produce hyaluronidase for similar purposes, to help them invade tissues. There are two main types of hyaluronidase, it turns out. Some break down hyaluronic acid into simple sugars. Others break it up into large chunks that act as an alarm signal to the immune system.
When it became clear that there were two types, Liu’s team searched genetic databases to see which type is found in which bacteria. They found the “simple sugars” type was the most common. The “large chunks” type was limited to a few free-living bacteria, which makes sense because they don’t need to worry about immune systems.
“The exception was acne,” says Liu. C. acnes jumped out to the researchers because it produces both types of hyaluronidase. More precisely, some strains of C. acne produce the simple-sugars type, while other produce the large-chunks one – none produce both, he says.
That made Liu wonder if this was connected to acne. Sure enough, the team showed in mouse studies that large-chunks strains of C. acnes cause acne-related inflammation, while the simple-sugars one slightly reduces inflammation. The team then went to show that a vaccine that stimulates the production of antibodies targeting only the large-chunks form of hyaluronidase could reduce acne in mice, as could inhibiting the enzyme with a small protein.
What isn’t clear is why some strains of C. acnes have evolved to trigger an immune response. One possibility is that it is a way to kill off some of their competitors, says Liu.
He thinks that in people, a vaccine against the large-chunks form of hyaluronidase would be most effective against the “more severe, red, angry type of acne lesion”.
“The ones that are hard to treat right now, those are the ones that we would target with a vaccine,” he says.
His findings might also help explain why antibiotics, which are commonly prescribed for acne, don’t work that well: they kill off the helpful C. acnes strains as well as the harmful ones. The other issue with antibiotics, of course, is that resistance can develop.
Another acne treatment called isotretinoin (Roaccutane) is more effective than antibiotics but has a long list of nasty side effects including causing birth defects, impotence and dry, itchy skin. How it works isn’t clear, though there is some evidence it alters the skin microbiome.
Acne vaccines promise to solve all these issues. They shouldn’t have any lasting side effects, nor should there be any issue with resistance, because the vaccines are targeting secreted proteins rather than directly targeting bacteria.
The fact that two competing approaches are being developed is great news for those with acne. If one vaccine doesn’t work, perhaps the other will. And it could be that both will work, or that targeting both CAMP and hyaluronidase simultaneously will prove even more effective than either alone. Maybe, just maybe, adolescence is about to get a little easier.

candidato.titulo: Xpanner launches autonomous pile driver for solar farm contruction
candidato.resumo: Xpanner's new X1 Piling R6 robot autonomously drives solar posts with one operator, improving placement accuracy while cutting on-site labor. The post Xpanner launches autonomous pile driver for solar farm contruction appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
Xpanner today announced the X1 Piling R6, a fully automated pile-driving robot built to autonomously install posts for utility-scale solar and battery energy storage, or BESS, sites. Supervised by a single operator, the system uses high-precision GNSS and onboard sensors to place each pile accurately, helping builders keep pace with new power demand despite a shortage of skilled crews.
The core of the robot is Xpanner’s Everstar R6 crawler base machine. The R6 is equipped with the Santa Fe Springs, Calif.-based company‘s automation stack with onboard sensors and controls to autonomously complete the pile driving process for each post.
Xpanner designs for simplified operation
An operator uploads a plan, then walks X1 Piling R6 machine to the row using a remote control interface. The operator supervises the construction as the machine drives each pile accurately.
The R6 can autonomously navigate to the subsequent pile locations using high-precision GNSS antennas and receivers, precision sensors, and the Xpanner-developed automation controller. One operator can remotely manage the installation process.
“Solar and BESS builders are racing to bring new power online for the grid and for AI data centers, and they can’t find enough skilled crews to keep up,” said Henri Lee, co-founder and CEO of Xpanner. “X1 lets one operator drive every pile plumb with a single touch, keeps people away from the mast, and logs each pile as it goes in. It takes the automation EPCs [engineering, procurement, and construction firms] already trust on PD10 and puts it on a more powerful, more versatile machine.”
X1 connects to Xpanner Connect, the company’s web-based project dashboard. Project teams can load the pile schedule and coordinates, assign machines, and set up a site in minutes.
As X1 works, it records each pile’s position, depth, and plumb and posts it to a live project map, replacing manual counts, phone calls, spreadsheets, and end-of-day reports. Managers can also monitor machine state, cycle counts, and alerts across the fleet without a site visit.
Xpanner said business model is a mixed capex/SaaS subscription model. Customers purchase (or rent) the X1 Piling robot and then license the automation software on a monthly subscription basis for each active technology.
According to the company, the subscription is not tied to a specific project, site, or number of piles driven. Rather, the customer pays for the technology while it is actively being used. Once piling operations or the applicable task is completed, the equipment and technology can be transferred to another project and activated as needed.
Xpanner handles initial installation, calibration, operator training, and technical support, while the contractor provides the equipment operators on-site.
Key features of the X1 Piling R6 robot
- Power for hard ground: The system includes a 97 kW (130 hp) engine and a high-frequency hydraulic hammer with up to 1,260 J (929 ft.-lb.) of impact energy and three energy settings to match soil conditions.
- Fine positioning without tramming: The guide rail slides 11.8 in. (300 mm) forward and back and 19.7 in. (500 mm) left and right, and the upper body rotates 180 degrees, putting the hammer on target from a single setup.
- Range of pile lengths: The X1 can drive piles up to 23 ft. (7.0 m) long, with a maximum driving depth of 15.7 ft. (4.8 m). Because the hammer lowers near the ground and piles can be driven flush to grade, one machine handles standard tracker piles, short motor piles, and BESS foundation piles without an adapter.
- Built for the field: Features include a mast that does not need disassembly for transport, a large fuel tank for long shifts, engine auto-idle, a large-capacity cooler, manual override, and e-stop.
- Multi-function mast (and potential capabilities): DTH drilling, auger drilling, and ground screwing on the same carrier, so one machine can pre-drill and drive.
The X1 Piling R6 is designed to work together with the X1 panel lift, which was released earlier this year, for autonomous solar panel installation.

texto_fonte:
Cuidado: excluir histórico de IA não apaga rastros em celulares Android
Por Viviane França |
Os pesquisadores do Instituto de Tecnologia da Geórgia (Georgia Tech), nos Estados Unidos, desenvolveram uma ferramenta que consegue recuperar conversas excluídas de assistentes de IA que funcionam localmente em celulares Android. A tecnologia, batizada de ORISA, identifica fragmentos de bate-papos que continuam na memória do aparelho mesmo após a exclusão pelo aplicativo.
Isso acontece porque apagar um bate-papo pela interface do aplicativo não remove imediatamente todos os dados armazenados na memória de trabalho (RAM) do celular. Com isso, a ferramenta também conseguiu reconstruir o contexto das conversas e criar uma nova sessão funcional do chatbot.
A pesquisa foi realizada no Laboratório de Inovação em Forense Cibernética do Georgia Tech e apresentada no 2026 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy. Para testar a ferramenta, a equipe liderada pelo doutorando Ken Xu criou um assistente fictício chamado Project Note Keeper no aplicativo de código aberto ChatterUI.
Os pesquisadores forneceram 100 fatos fictícios ao assistente antes de excluir a conversa. Naquele momento, o modelo conseguia acessar ativamente apenas 14 informações devido ao limite de memória. O ORISA, porém, recuperou 26 fatos armazenados no celular e criou uma nova sessão capaz de responder a perguntas sobre o projeto.
O experimento também mostrou que a ferramenta consegue resgatar informações que já haviam saído da janela de contexto da IA. Embora o modelo não conseguisse mais consultar esses fatos durante a conversa original, os dados ainda permaneciam na memória do dispositivo e puderam ser recuperados pelo ORISA.
A equipe validou o desempenho da ferramenta em 60 configurações de teste, com 10 aplicativos Android e três modelos de IA. No entanto, segundo os pesquisadores, a recuperação fica mais difícil à medida que outras atividades do sistema sobrescrevem os dados antigos na memória do dispositivo.
O artigo Recovering and Rehosting Mobile Local LLM Conversations and Contexts via Memory Forensics também tem como autores os doutorandos David Oygenblik, Runze Zhang e Mingxuan Yao, o cientista de pesquisa Muhammad Ibrahim e o professor associado Brendan Saltaformaggio.
Ferramenta ajuda em investigações, mas levanta alertas de privacidade
O ORISA foi desenvolvido para auxiliar em investigações criminais e perícias digitais. A ferramenta consegue recuperar informações compartilhadas com assistentes de IA e as respostas recebidas, o que pode ajudar a esclarecer casos em que orientações de um chatbot tenham causado danos. No entanto, a tecnologia não é um aplicativo comercial ou público para usuários comuns restaurarem conversas apagadas, mas um recurso para análise forense de dispositivos.
A descoberta também levanta questões sobre a privacidade de quem usa assistentes de IA com processamento local, como o Google AI Edge Gallery e o ChatterUI. Essas ferramentas executam modelos no próprio celular, o que reduz a necessidade de enviar informações pessoais para servidores na nuvem. Ainda assim, apagar uma conversa não garante que todos os seus registros desapareçam imediatamente, pois fragmentos do histórico podem permanecer na memória do aparelho.
A recuperação depende de acesso forense à memória e ao armazenamento do dispositivo. Por isso, o estudo não indica que qualquer pessoa consiga restaurar conversas apagadas com facilidade. Os pesquisadores também não investigaram se bate-papos com assistentes de IA baseados na nuvem poderiam ser recuperados por técnicas semelhantes.
Se você gostou do conteúdo, talvez também se interesse por conferir “O que é "IA local"? Entenda como funcionam as ferramentas que rodam no seu PC”.

candidato.titulo: Apple anuncia MacBook Pro e iMac de 24 polegadas com chip M6; veja preços
candidato.resumo: Novo MacBook Pro de 14 polegadas promete ainda até 24 horas de autonomia. Já novo iMac de 24 polegadas traz sete opções de cores. Apple anuncia MacBook Pro e iMac de 24 polegadas com chip M6; veja preços

texto_fonte:
Resumo
- A Apple anunciou o MacBook Pro de 14 polegadas e o iMac de 24 polegadas com chip M6, que oferece até 30% mais desempenho gráfico e até 25% mais desempenho em IA em relação ao M5.
- O MacBook Pro tem bateria que dura até 24 horas e carregamento rápido de 50% em 30 minutos; preço inicial é de R$ 24.999.
- O iMac de 24 polegadas tem tela Retina 4,5K e preço inicial de R$ 17.999.
A Apple escolheu esta semana para fazer uma série de anúncios de produtos. Começou com o iPad Mini com tela OLED. Agora, nesta terça-feira (27/10), a companhia revelou dois Macs com chip M6: um MacBook Pro de 14 polegadas e um iMac de 24 polegadas. No Brasil, os preços começam em R$ 17.999.
O que há de interessante no novo MacBook Pro?
O Apple M6 é um chip com até 12 núcleos de CPU e 12 núcleos de GPU, sendo que estes últimos são complementados com aceleradores de inteligência artificial. Também para lidar com tarefas de IA, o chip conta com uma implementação do Neural Engine com dois blocos de 16 núcleos.
Eis o efeito: o M6 oferece até 30% mais desempenho gráfico, bem como até 25% mais desempenho em IA em relação ao M5. Isso deixa claro que o MacBook Pro continua apto a lidar com tarefas que demandam altas cargas de trabalho.
Isso sem abrir mão da autonomia: ainda de acordo com a Apple, o MacBook Pro de 14 polegadas conta com uma bateria que dura até 24 horas com uma recarga completa. Trata-se do maior tempo de autonomia já registrado na linha. Para completar, a carga pode chegar a 50% de capacidade com apenas 30 minutos de tomada.
Falando dos demais recursos, o novo MacBook Pro também conta com uma tela Liquid Retina XDR (LCD com mini-LED) de 14 polegadas que alcança brilho de pico de 1.600 nits em HDR e, opcionalmente, com vidro “nano-texture”, que reduz os reflexos para melhorar a percepção de qualidade de imagem.
A frente também abriga uma câmera de 12 megapixels com tecnologia Center Stage, que usa IA para manter o usuário centralizado na imagem durante chamadas de vídeo.
Outros atributos de destaque incluem:
- conectividade Wi-Fi 7 e Bluetooth 6.0 via chip N1, Thunderbolt 4 (três portas), HDMI, MagSafe 3, leitor de cartões SDXC, conexão para fones
- memória RAM unificada de 16 GB a 32 GB
- armazenamento de até 8 TB
- sistema operacional macOS 27
E o que há de legal no novo iMac de 24 polegadas?
O novo iMac de 24 polegadas traz o mesmo chip M6 do novo MacBook Pro, podendo ter dez ou 12 núcleos de CPU e GPU, o que significa que desempenho também é um ponto forte do modelo, principalmente no âmbito da inteligência artificial.
Mas, talvez, o maior destaque fique para a tela, que consiste em um painel Retina (LCD) de 24 polegadas com resolução 4,5K. O componente suporta ainda até 500 nits de brilho e mais de 1 bilhão de cores. A câmera de 12 megapixels com Center Stage está por lá. O vidro “nano-texture” também é uma opção aqui.
Outras características incluem:
- de 256 GB a 2 TB de armazenamento
- de 16 GB a 32 GB de memória unificada
- quatro portas Thunderbolt 4 na traseira
- conectividade Wi-Fi 7 e Bluetooth 6.0 via chip N1
- sistema operacional macOS 27
Preços e disponibilidade dos novos Macs no Brasil
O novo MacBook Pro de 14 polegadas já aparece no site brasileiro da Apple, mas ainda não há informação sobre data de disponibilidade. Por lá, o preço parte de R$ 24.999, podendo variar de acordo com a configuração escolhida (o chip pode ser o M6, o M5 Pro ou o M5 Max, por exemplo).
Sobre o novo iMac de 24 polegadas, a novidade também não teve data de lançamento confirmada para o Brasil, mas custará a partir de R$ 17.999 por aqui. Haverá sete opções de cores: azul, roxo, rosa, laranja, amarelo, verde e prateado.
Nos Estados Unidos, ambos os produtos começarão a ser vendidos oficialmente a partir de 6 de novembro, mas a pré-venda terá início amanhã (28/10).
Vale lembrar que, ontem, a Apple anunciou o iPad Mini com tela OLED e chip A20 Pro. Para amanhã, podemos esperar o anúncio de um MacBook com tela touch. Fiquemos de olho.

texto_fonte:
Press Release
Dead star and planetary bodies: astronomers spot unique disc of debris that foretells Solar System’s future
27 October 2026
Astronomers using the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope (ESO’s VLT) have found a rare disc of debris around a dead star that provides a glimpse of what may happen to our Solar System. Unlike in similar systems previously found, the debris — the leftovers of planets that once orbited the star — is organised in a double disc, the two parts separated by a clear gap. The disc appears to be shaped by two planetary bodies, one possibly as big as Pluto, that have survived the violent death of the star.
“We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disc and potentially two surviving planetesimals,” says Nicola Gentille Fusillo, astronomer at the Università degli Studi di Trieste, Italy, and lead author of the study published this week in Nature Astronomy. The central star of this system is the white dwarf J1328−1450, the dense and burnt-out core left behind when a star similar to our Sun ran out of fuel.
As stars like the Sun enter the final stages of their life, they expand and shed their outer layers, engulfing and destroying nearby planets. The surviving rocky bodies can break apart forming a disc around the central, dead star. However, the disc around J1328−1450 is different from those observed around other dead stars: instead of having only one ring of vaporised planetary rubble, the star is surrounded by two concentric debris rings.
“The structure we see in this system is particularly intriguing because the two gaseous rings are remarkably stable and remain separated by a gap,” says co-author Felipe Lagos-Vilches, an astronomer at the University of Warwick, UK and at the Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María in Chile. “The system is a rare glimpse of the violent, chaotic process by which a planetary system meets its end, and it hints that dead stars can have disc structures far more complex than previously realised,” adds Gentile Fusillo, who is also affiliated with the INAF-Astronomical Observatory of Trieste.
According to the team, this complex double structure is likely maintained by two surviving planet-like bodies, on separate orbits. They estimate that the one in the inner ring is the size of a typical asteroid, a few kilometres in diameter, while the outer one could be as large as Pluto, or even our Moon.
All known debris discs around white dwarfs have been identified by the same observational signature, which indicates the presence of a single, flat, rotating disc. But the new observations, made with the X-Shooter instrument on ESO’s VLT in Chile’s Atacama Desert, show that the J1328−1450 system breaks this pattern completely, revealing instead the unique fingerprint of a double disc.
The observations also reveal that elements such as calcium, oxygen, magnesium and iron are present in the disc, indicating a composition similar to that of rocky planetary material found in our own Solar System. Moreover, the data indicate that the two rings in the disc in fact have rather different compositions, with the inner ring rich in magnesium gas and the outer largely stripped of it. This suggests that the planetesimals that feed the rings originated from two planets with different compositions. An alternative explanation is that they are the result of different parts of a celestial body, like the crust and core of a planet.
Our Solar System could meet a similar end, as our Sun will, in a far future, become a white dwarf in a process that may destroy Earth. “The system therefore offers a remarkable glimpse of what the future of planetary systems, including systems like our own, might look like,” concludes Lagos-Vilches.

texto_fonte:
Insider Brief
- IBM researchers linked two 120-qubit quantum processors with four superconducting cables, demonstrating connections that could support larger modular quantum computers.
- The links achieved average quantum state-transfer fidelity of 99% and enabled operations and entanglement between qubits on separate processors.
- Complete operations between processors averaged 94.75% fidelity, with further improvements needed in qubit stability, magnetic shielding and manufacturing before scaling the approach.
IBM researchers connected two quantum processors through four superconducting cables, demonstrating a way to build larger quantum computers from separate chips.
The links transferred quantum states with an average fidelity of 99% and supported operations between computing elements on different processors, according to a study posted on the preprint server arXiv. The team also created entangled states spanning the chips, including two pairs generated at the same time through neighboring connections.
The results address a practical problem in quantum computing: how to make separate processors work together without losing the fragile information that gives the machines their potential. Connecting modules could let developers expand a computer beyond the limits of a single chip.
The experiment also shows that work remains. Complete operations between the processors had an average fidelity of 94.75%, below the performance of the state transfers alone. Only a subset of the computing elements on each processor was wired and measured.
Building a Computer Across Chips
The researchers connected two IBM Nighthawk R1 superconducting processors, each containing 120 qubits. Qubits are the basic units of quantum information, but their useful properties can be disrupted by energy loss, environmental interference and imperfect controls.
A modular computer would divide the work among processors, using quantum connections to coordinate operations across them. Those links must preserve quantum states and support entanglement, a relationship in which separate qubits share a joint quantum state.
The IBM team used four aluminum coaxial cables, each about 80 centimeters long, to bridge the processors. The cables operated as superconducting microwave links inside the system’s ultracold environment.
The distance reflects the physical demands of installing processors, cooling equipment and control wiring, according to the study. These are connections within a quantum computing system, rather than links intended to carry information across a conventional telecommunications network.
Earlier experiments have transferred quantum states and generated entanglement through superconducting cables. Many of those experiments used modules containing only a few qubits and a single connection between processors, the researchers write.
IBM’s contribution centers on operating several connections between large processors with a cable attachment designed for more densely connected systems. The researchers describe the work as — to their knowledge — the first demonstration of a multichannel quantum interconnect between large superconducting quantum processors.
The 120-qubit chip size does not mean the experiment coordinated all 240 qubits, as the team wired and measured only selected qubits near the connections to speed development.
Transferring States and Creating Entanglement
Each connection used dedicated qubits at the cable’s ends to move quantum information between modules. Adjustable coupling devices controlled how those qubits interacted with the cable.
The researchers measured state-transfer performance in both directions using network benchmarking, a method that separates transfer errors from errors associated with preparing and measuring the qubits.
All four links achieved state-transfer fidelities of at least 98.86%. The best reached 99.29%, with an uncertainty of 0.07 percentage points. Fidelity measures how closely an operation or prepared state matches its intended result.
The team then used the connections to perform controlled-Z gates between ordinary computing qubits on separate processors. A controlled-Z gate changes the relationship between two qubits’ quantum states and can help create entanglement.
That complete operation required more steps than transferring a state across a cable. It combined two state transfers, three local two-qubit gates and additional single-qubit controls.
The extra steps introduced additional opportunities for error. Average fidelity for the distant gates was 94.75%, while the best reached 96.42%, with an uncertainty of 0.28 percentage points, according to the paper.
Using those gates, the researchers generated entangled pairs across the processors. They also generated two pairs simultaneously through adjacent links. Both pairs remained entangled, although one showed a measurable decline in fidelity during simultaneous operation.
The experiment extended entanglement to groups of four and six computing qubits distributed across the chips. These larger states show that the connections can support operations beyond the dedicated qubits at the cable ends.
The four-qubit state had a measured fidelity of 77.23%, while the six-qubit state reached 67.67%. After statistical correction for measurement errors, those figures rose to 91.70% and 90.87%, respectively.
While correcting measurement results does not improve the underlying physical operation, both states nevertheless exceeded the threshold needed to establish genuine entanglement across the group without that correction, the researchers reported.
A Connection That Can Survive Cooling
Part of the work focused on assembly rather than quantum operations.
The cables attached perpendicular to the processor surface, a shape intended to accommodate more connections. Earlier IBM designs placed the cable-to-chip connection parallel to the surface, creating difficulties for reliability and denser packing, according to the study.
The new arrangement used indium-to-indium pressure bonds made at room temperature after both processor modules had been mounted in the cryogenic system. A spring-loaded holder installed two cable connections at once, using screws and visual alignment.
All four links remained operational through three cycles of warming and cooling without adjustments to their connections.
That durability is required because a modular machine will need maintenance and reconfiguration over its lifetime, the researchers write. However, the team did not disconnect and reconnect the bonds in this experiment. Their suitability for repeated reconnection may be the focus of further testing.
The researchers also identified a source of cable loss: magnetic fields present while the aluminum cooled into its superconducting state.
In controlled tests, the cable’s ability to retain microwave energy declined substantially as the magnetic field during cooling increased. Changing the field after the cable had become superconducting did not reverse the effect.
The team added magnetic shielding around the cables. Two layers were needed, and the researchers described the shielding braid as a temporary solution. The physical mechanism behind the observed loss remains unresolved, although the paper identifies trapped magnetic fields as a possible explanation.
Reducing the Remaining Errors
The study points to several routes for improving performance, while distinguishing projections from measured results.
An error model attributed about 77% of the measured state-transfer error to the limited persistence of quantum states in the cable and its dedicated qubits. The largest modeled contribution came from the qubits losing a stable phase relationship, a process known as dephasing.
The researchers intentionally omitted some fabrication and processing steps known to improve qubit performance to accelerate development. They therefore argue that the observed qubit limitations are not inherent to the cable-link approach.
With improved qubit coherence, their model placed state-transfer fidelity between 99.68% and 99.77% across the four links. Those figures are modeled limits under specified conditions, not experimental results.
The team also identified a design change that could reduce the cost of distant operations: integrating the connection elements directly into the processor’s computing lattice. That would eliminate some of the intermediate operations required by the present arrangement, according to the paper.
The next challenge is to turn four working links into many reproducible connections while improving fidelity, shielding and manufacturability. The experiment establishes a component for that effort. Demonstrating a larger machine that repeatedly uses those connections for reliable, error-corrected computation remains ahead.

However, it is not — nor is this article, itself — official peer-review publications. Peer-review is an important step in the scientific process to verify results.

Apple is updating two more computers to its M6 system-on-chip. The base 14-inch MacBook Pro and the iMac lineup are getting the company's latest processor ahead of tomorrow's "Pro and Tell" event in Los Angeles.
These devices are retaining the same designs that they've had for years. The computers will be available for pre-order on Wednesday at 10:10 a.m. PT (1:10 p.m. ET) and will ship on Nov. 6. The M6 in the MacBook Pro will be configured with 12 CPU cores and 12 GPU cores, alongside dual neural engines for certain on-device AI workloads. On the iMac, there will also be a cut-down option with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU.
The MacBook Pro will be configurable with up to 32GB of RAM and is being updated with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 using Apple's N1 networking chip. The iMac is also getting those networking benefits, as well as a 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet port. Like previous iMacs, the number of ports you get is tied to the chip, with two Thunderbolt 4 ports with the base chip or four with the option with more cores.
It's no surprise that Apple is pushing both of these as AI-forward machines, both with the new chips and the recently released Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features in macOS 27 Golden Gate.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 will start at $1,999 ($1,899 with education discount), while the iMac will begin at $1,499 ($1,449 with education discount) for the 10-core CPU/GPU configuration and $1,699 ($1,599 with education discount) for the full chip.

texto_fonte:
I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
My experiment with an IEEE journal revealed AI’s threats to scholarly publishing
Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up.
According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025.
Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it, these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually.
“It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz, IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.”
Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record?
Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.
The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?
Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.
Round 1: Creating the Forgery
To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.
Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.
Luigi Avantaggiato
I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.
My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.
I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.
At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.
What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”
Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.
Round 1: Attempt to Publish
Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI
Jorge Cuadel Calle
I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.
ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI
1. Choose a research topic 
I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.
2. Break the paper into pieces 
The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.
3. Keep steering the LLMs 
When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”
4. Build and polish the paper 
After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.
5. Put it to the test 
I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.
→ CAUGHT 
IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.
ROUND 2: FARS
1. Give FARS a research topic 
I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.
2. Authorize the experiment 
With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.
3. Let FARS do the research 
FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.
4. Tell FARS to write the paper 
Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.
5. Put it to the test 
I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.
→ CAUGHT 
The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.
Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?
As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!
In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”
Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.
The AI Arms Race
On one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.
These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.
It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.
Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.
Burden on Academics
Mahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.
Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed.
What Gave Away My AI Papers
Round 1: The Fake Paper
Created with free versions of ChatGPT and Gemini
Ghost citations
Many references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated.
Questionable scientific claims
An expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable.
Too many acronyms
The expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract.
Round 2: The AI-Research Paper
Created by the autonomous research system FARS
Too many preprints
The references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints.
Nonsense in a figure
One technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.”
AI artifacts
Another figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots.
PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record.
Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky, cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles.
Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.”
Blurred Lines
My homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?
Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System), AutoResearchClaw, The AIScientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher, and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.
What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?
Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw, for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery.
The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.”
FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours, was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma. “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su, Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.)
Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test.
Round 2: Using an AI Science Engine
FARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously.
Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time.
With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours.
At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney.
Round 2: Attempt to Publish
Because FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one.
“Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem.
In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated.
Automation Changing the Landscape
Automated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process.
“FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.”
Benjamin Skuse's experiment raised a bigger question: What counts as legitimate scientific research in the age of AI?
Luigi Avantaggiato
In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?”
A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future?
Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.”
In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?”

Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent.
Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud.

The unexpected key to extending EV battery life found in 'oxygen release'
What if a battery could become more powerful as it ages? Much like wine developing a deeper flavor over time, researchers in Korea have uncovered the mechanism behind a battery material that can deliver greater usable capacity after repeated charging and discharging.
A research team led by professor Jihyun Hong (Department of Battery Engineering at POSTECH) with Dr. Gukhyeon Lim and a team led by professor Kyu-Young Park (Department of Battery Engineering & Materials Science and Engineering at POSTECH) with doctoral student Hojun Lee have identified the origins of performance degradation in manganese-based cathode materials, which are considered promising candidates for next-generation electric vehicle batteries.
The team proposed a new strategy for turning what has traditionally been regarded as a weakness of the material into a potential performance advantage.
The study was published in Energy & Environmental Science.
Lower costs, persistent degradation
The electric vehicle industry is actively searching for cost-effective next-generation battery materials capable of competing with inexpensive lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries manufactured in China. One of the most promising candidates is the lithium- and manganese-rich layered oxide (LMRO) cathode.
LMROs require less expensive nickel and cobalt while storing approximately 20% more energy than conventional nickel-based cathode materials, making them attractive for batteries that could be both less expensive and capable of longer driving ranges.
However, LMROs have a critical drawback. Their capacity gradually decreases with repeated charging and discharging, while their operating voltage also declines. Previous studies attempting to identify the cause have reported different final structures inside the cathode, leaving the fundamental mechanism governing these structural changes unresolved.
Oxygen loss drives structural disorder
The POSTECH team examined how the internal structure of the cathode evolved over hundreds of charge-discharge cycles. Initially, lithium and transition-metal atoms are neatly arranged in separate layers, resembling bricks stacked in an orderly wall. As charging continues, however, some of the oxygen atoms that stabilize this framework gradually escape from the material. This is similar to a well-organized drawer whose contents gradually become jumbled over time.
As these oxygen atoms are removed, lithium and transition-metal atoms begin to migrate across their original layers and mix with one another. Eventually, the highly ordered layered structure transforms into a disordered rocksalt structure, in which the cations no longer follow their original long-range ordering.
The researchers discovered that the amount of oxygen lost from the material acts as a key trigger determining how extensively the internal structure becomes disordered. They further demonstrated that oxygen loss can be controlled by how deeply the battery is charged—in other words, by how high the charging voltage is raised. Deeper charging led to greater oxygen loss, while the resulting oxygen vacancies progressively accumulated and drove structural rearrangement within the cathode.
Turning disorder into usable capacity
The most surprising finding came afterward. Oxygen loss would normally be regarded as a clear sign of battery degradation. However, as the cathode became disordered and transformed into a new structure, additional pathways through which lithium ions could move were created. As a result, usable capacity increased.
By carefully controlling the degree of oxygen loss and the resulting structural evolution, the researchers demonstrated that the cathode retained 98.4% of its initial performance even after more than 200 charge-discharge cycles, showing long-term durability.
Structural disorder in battery materials has traditionally been regarded as an undesirable aging phenomenon that should be avoided. This study, however, demonstrates that when such structural evolution is precisely controlled, it can instead become a design tool for improving battery performance.
Hong said, "From an industrial perspective, our study shows that battery degradation can be delayed and battery lifetime extended simply by controlling parameters such as operating temperature and the surface environment." He added, "By regulating oxygen loss and thereby either promoting or suppressing structural disorder, it may become possible to design next-generation electric vehicle batteries optimized for different applications."
Park, a co-corresponding author of the study, said, "By integrating precise materials characterization with computational materials science, we were able to address a problem that had remained unresolved for nearly two decades. The collaborative research environment within POSTECH's Department of Battery Engineering, which encourages interaction and cooperation among researchers through the Specialized Graduate School Program, played a decisive role in making this work possible."
Publication details

candidato.resumo: A empresa de cibersegurança WatchGuard identificou um malware que usa elementos legítimos do Windows e arquivos executáveis de programas reais para invadir computadores de vítimas. No Brasil, o golpe começa a partir de e-mails falsos sobre cobranças de cartórios . As tentativas de phishing levam as vítimas a sites fraudulentos e induzem ao download de scripts VBScript maliciosos . Os arquivos também podem usar uma técnica para distribuir um diretório malicioso dentro de um arquivo executável legítimo do Windows . A pesquisa identificou a técnica em arquivos como ngentask.exe, do Microsoft .NET Framework , e vlc.exe, do famoso reprodutor de mídia VLC . Ambos se passam como executáveis legítimos para instalar um programa no Windows, mas estão corrompidos. O script se conecta com um trojan chamado Overlord RAT, no qual é possível controlar o computador remotamente após instalar um vírus no sistema. A análise de código da ameaça registrou algumas verificações de referências a apps de bancos e instituições financeiras brasileiras. Os dados indicam que a execução do malware pode considerar referências que miram esses serviços, mas não há evidências de invasão ou roubo de dados de cliente

Vírus no Brasil usa ferramentas autênticas do Windows e o VLC para invadir conta bancária
Por André Lourenti Magalhães • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
A empresa de cibersegurança WatchGuard identificou um malware que usa elementos legítimos do Windows e arquivos executáveis de programas reais para invadir computadores de vítimas. No Brasil, o golpe começa a partir de e-mails falsos sobre cobranças de cartórios.
As tentativas de phishing levam as vítimas a sites fraudulentos e induzem ao download de scripts VBScript maliciosos. Os arquivos também podem usar uma técnica para distribuir um diretório malicioso dentro de um arquivo executável legítimo do Windows.
A pesquisa identificou a técnica em arquivos como ngentask.exe, do Microsoft .NET Framework, e vlc.exe, do famoso reprodutor de mídia VLC. Ambos se passam como executáveis legítimos para instalar um programa no Windows, mas estão corrompidos.
O script se conecta com um trojan chamado Overlord RAT, no qual é possível controlar o computador remotamente após instalar um vírus no sistema.
A análise de código da ameaça registrou algumas verificações de referências a apps de bancos e instituições financeiras brasileiras. Os dados indicam que a execução do malware pode considerar referências que miram esses serviços, mas não há evidências de invasão ou roubo de dados de clientes.
Malwares também miram contas bancárias
O relatório da WatchGuard também identificou campanhas de malware em Portugal. Uma delas envolve o trojan bancário Lampion, usado para invadir contas em serviços financeiros.
Os arquivos fraudulentos também usam elementos legítimos do Windows, como arquivos DLL, em tentativa de burlar o monitoramento do Microsoft Defender.
Para evitar ser vítima nesse tipo de golpe, é muito importante desconfiar de mensagens muito alarmantes, principalmente aquelas com arquivos anexados. Evite fazer o download e mantenha sempre um antivírus atualizado.
